title: AES-128 Bit faults: chosen byte (Giraud, AES2004 proceedings published 2005)

target.description: Full AES-128; recover the complete 128-bit final round key. Inverse AES-128 key expansion yields the master key.

setting.key_relation: One fixed secret AES master key; no related-key oracle.
setting.key_population: Keys of the stated AES implementation without a weak-key restriction; fault protections are outside the model.
setting.plaintext_model: Repeat encryptions of the same plaintext under the same key; retain its correct ciphertext as a reference. Counts of faulty ciphertexts exclude that reusable reference unless explicitly stated otherwise.

fault_model.target: The state entering the final round, not a key-schedule fault.
fault_model.granularity: Exactly one bit is flipped in one state byte per useful execution.
fault_model.timing: Immediately before SubBytes in the final round 10, at state M^9.
fault_model.location: The attacker chooses the byte to disturb, but not the bit difference within that byte.
fault_model.value_control: The flipped bit is unknown; candidates cover the eight possible one-bit differences.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty output is matched to the same fixed-input correct reference; useful faults, random-location ciphertexts and physical executions have distinct accounting.

assumptions: The final AES round omits MixColumns; a single-bit state fault produces one nonzero output byte.
The reported outcome and data budget use the paper's candidate-filtering model; no numerical whole-key success rate is inferred from a byte-level statistic.

time.note: No numerical whole-endpoint runtime is reported for this version and endpoint.

data.note: Section 5's average with selectable affected byte, separate from the unknown-location headline.

memory.note: The article describes counters or candidate lists without a numerical peak-memory budget.

preprocessing.note: No separate reusable preprocessing-time budget is reported. The Appendix A 8×2^8 equation tests per useful output are a component count, not a complete attack cost.

success.description: No numerical success is supplied for this full last-round-key endpoint at the recorded budget. AppendixA gives local one-byte random-subset estimates50%/97%, not a joint16-byte rate. Section5 reports35 chosen-byte faults on average and Section3 fewer than50 random-location faults; expected counts do not specify finite-budget byte coverage or whole-output success.  JMR07 SectionIV-B.2/TableI and footnote* add only unprotected one-byte software observations:71% after2 random faults,91% after3 and97% after4. These are different from Giraud's random13-subset model and from the protected implementation row; no16-byte joint event, location-collection distribution or fixed-budget whole-output rate is supplied. The35-fault figure stays an average and is not replaced by48faults.

review.scope: Original Section3/Section5/AppendixA and newly acquired JMR07 SectionIII-A/IV-B.2/TableI/footnote* checked. Later software observations quantify one byte only and lack trial denominators/full sampling protocols. No composition into native35-average/<50 or parallel-byte full-output success is justified. Original costs, settings, targets, components and conflicts are unchanged; no new full-paper audit.

components.description: Section3 Equation6 / AppendixA Equation32: for an effective single-bit fault, complete enumeration includes the actual state byte. Inclusion is not uniqueness, byte coverage, or last-round-key recovery.

AppendixA Equation33 approximates two independently uniform13-element wrong-candidate subsets of255 values. Its rounded50% is for one byte after two useful single-bit faults, not the whole key or physical fault acquisition.

AppendixA Equation34 / Section3 gives rounded97% for one byte after three useful single-bit faults under the source random-subset model. The proceedings says97%, not98%; it is not a proved distribution of actual fixed-input AES fault candidates.

evidence.locator: Section 5 p.38; Section 3 pp.31–32 (last-subkey target and longer-key extension)
evidence.interpretation: Version-specific endpoint retaining its target, prior information, fault controls and native sample accounting.

evidence.interpretation: Later original-attack single-byte simulations are relevant new evidence, but do not quantify the complete last-round/master-key output at this record's native budget. They also do not establish independence across bytes, fault acquisition or a stopping distribution. The original35average/<50 and all old local components remain, with the primary still not quantified.

limitations: Useful faulty ciphertext counts do not automatically include ineffective physical injections or calibration attempts.
The article does not supply a measured success frequency, runtime or peak memory for every target and parameter choice.
